Codillon with refinement types · gcd as a type · gallery of ten angles

One type, ten pictures

A refinement type is a set of values. The output of Euclid's algorithm can be given a type that pins it down completely:

Gcd(a, b) = { g ∈ ℕ | Div(g) = Div(a) ∩ Div(b) } Div(n) is the set of divisors of n, and Div(0) = ℕ because every number divides 0. Equivalently: g ∣ a, g ∣ b, and every common divisor d of a and b divides g.

It is a dependent type: a different set for every pair (a, b). It is a singleton: the only inhabitant is the gcd. And Euclid's loop (x, y) → (y, x mod y) inhabits it because each step leaves Div(x) ∩ Div(y) unchanged, and once y = 0 that set is just Div(x).

Every picture on this page is a different way of seeing that one set. Ten agents were each given one visual angle and the same brief: a reader should understand the type by looking, with the prose switched off. The figures were then audited number by number (see the audit log); the strongest figure of each angle is shown large and the rest can be enlarged.

purple: the type, a setnavy: a concrete value or run dark red: a violation (type error)indigo: unknowngray: context

The example used everywhere: a = 12, b = 8

Part I · five angles

What the type is

Five pictures of the same set, from the most literal to the most algebraic. Each has to make two things visible: the common divisors Div(a) ∩ Div(b), and why exactly one g has that set as its own divisors. Each also draws a wrong candidate, g = 2 (too small: it misses the common divisor 4) or g = 8 (too big: 8 does not divide 12), as a type error.

02

Pins in sockets

angle 02 · divisor strips on a number line · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Gcd(a, b) is the one number whose row of divisors fills every common-divisor socket exactly: no socket left empty, no pin spilling outside.

Encoding

  • column → a candidate divisor d = 0, 1, 2, …
  • navy pin → d divides this row’s number
  • purple socket → d is a common divisor of a and b
  • hollow dark-red socket → a common divisor the candidate misses
  • crossed dark-red pin → a divisor of the candidate that is not common

What it hides

A literal number line only works for small numbers, and divisors appear as unrelated dots, so the order structure behind “greatest” stays implicit.

Audit

No wrong numbers. Fixed: a heading claimed all g in 0…12 were tested (7 are drawn); three “↑” pointers sat under the wrong columns; “0 spills” read as “divisor 0 spills”.

The interactive version of this picture is §1 of gcd-as-a-type.

06

Conjuncts as overlapping regions

angle 06 · refinement as nested predicate regions · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Each conjunct of Gcd(a, b) carves a region out of ℕ; the three regions meet in exactly one number, and dropping any conjunct lets an impostor in.

Encoding

  • solid circle → P₁: g ∣ a
  • dashed circle → P₂: g ∣ b
  • dotted circle → P₃: every common divisor divides g
  • number pill → which conjuncts that value satisfies
  • dark-red region or pill → a value a weakened spec wrongly admits

What it hides

Same-sized circles hide that Div(a) is finite while P₃ and ℕ are infinite, and that P₃ is computed from P₁ ∩ P₂ rather than being an independent set.

Audit

No wrong numbers: all 83 number pills sit in the right compartment (checked against the circle geometry). Fixed: incomplete pill lists for (1071, 462), a wrong reason for the empty compartment, a garbled leak sentence, a footer claiming every step only removes divisors, and eight overlaps.

01

The top of two cones

angle 01 · divisibility lattice · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

In the divisibility lattice Div(a) and Div(b) are downward cones; Gcd(a, b) is the single node whose own cone is exactly their overlap.

Encoding

  • node position → prime exponents: up-left ×2, up-right ×3
  • arrow u → v → v = u·p, so u ∣ v
  • dashed hull → Div(a) or Div(b): everything below the input
  • purple capsule → Div(a) ∩ Div(b), the target cone
  • dark-red cone → Div(g) of a wrong candidate

What it hides

It stays readable for two primes only, a mod step jumps across the lattice instead of following edges, and fig. 5’s shrinking cones are true of this run, not in general.

Audit

No wrong numbers (10 cover edges of Div(24), every hull, every candidate). Fixed: Div(2) drawn in indigo, the colour reserved for “unknown”; three label collisions; two overflowing text lines.

03

Prime-exponent boxes

angle 03 · prime-exponent space · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Plot each number by its exponents of 2 and 3: Div(n) becomes the box below n, and Gcd(a, b) is the one corner whose box is exactly the overlap.

Encoding

  • grid point (i, j) → the number 2ⁱ·3ʲ
  • dashed and dotted boxes → Div(a) and Div(b)
  • purple box → Div(a) ∩ Div(b): the box below the componentwise min
  • double-ringed corner → g, the only inhabitant
  • dark-red box or hatched cell → a candidate that overflows or falls short

What it hides

It needs factorizations Euclid never computes, a remainder can raise an exponent (1071 mod 462 = 147 = 3·7²), and 0 has no point, so Div(0) = ℕ is only a drawing convention.

Audit

No wrong numbers (all factorizations and box extents read from the SVG). Fixed: “outer box shrinks toward the corner”, which is false at both steps; “{3, 6, 12} ∤ 8” applied ∤ to a set; three label collisions.

07

The generator of an ideal

angle 07 · Bézout / ideal view · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

The combinations ax + by are exactly the multiples of one number g; Gcd(a, b) = {g}, the step of that lattice and its first positive point.

Encoding

  • purple dot on ℤ → a value ax + by some (x, y) reaches
  • double-ringed dot → the generator g
  • shaded box (0, g) → the gap no combination lands in
  • navy arc or (x, y) label → a Bézout certificate
  • dark-red ✕ or dashed ? → off a wrong grid, or unreachable

What it hides

It needs signed coefficients in ℤ while the program works in ℕ, and it never shows the divisor sets the type is defined by.

Audit

No wrong numbers (every certificate, all 49 lattice values, all 13 fiber lines). Fixed: the type was written {g | g > 0 ∧ …}, which excludes Gcd(0, 0) = {0}; “invariant!” labelled a Bézout witness; five overlaps.

Part II · one angle

How it depends on its inputs

A dependent type is a family of sets, one per input. Angle 08 is the one picture whose subject is that family itself; most other angles show dependence too, as small multiples of a few pairs (see the “shows dependence” column of the comparison).

08

A family of singleton fibers

angle 08 · dependent type family · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Gcd(a, b) is not one set but a family: over each input pair sits the singleton {gcd(a, b)}, and a result must land in the fiber over its own inputs.

Encoding

  • grid cell (a, b) → one index of the family, labelled gcd(a, b)
  • vertical line over an input → the ambient return type ℕ
  • purple ring on that line → the fiber Gcd(a, b), one element
  • navy dot → a returned value
  • dark-red ✕ → a value that belongs to another pair’s fiber

What it hides

Every fiber is a singleton, so “fiber” and “value” blur; the plane’s tints lump several gcds together; the divisor sets that explain membership live in side panels.

Audit

No wrong numbers (all 289 and 484 plane cells, the period-8 slice, both trajectories). Fixed: four labels that called the wrong thing the fiber (a whole ℕ line, the set Div(x) ∩ Div(y), a column with rejected values); two overflows.

Part III · three angles

Why Euclid’s program inhabits it

The proof has one lemma and three obligations: a step (x, y) → (y, x mod y) keeps Div(x) ∩ Div(y); the loop starts inside the invariant, stays inside it, and makes y smaller; and at y = 0 the invariant pins x to the type. The tiling shows the lemma, the state space shows the loop, and the derivation shows how the obligations compose.

04

Euclid’s square tiling

angle 04 · Euclid’s rectangle tiling · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

A common divisor is a square tile that fills the a×b rectangle exactly; cutting y×y squares off keeps every such tile, down to the largest one, the gcd.

Encoding

  • navy rectangle → the pair (a, b) or state (x, y), to scale
  • purple d×d grid → a common divisor: it tiles both sides
  • dark-red hatched overhang → d does not divide a side
  • dashed cut → one Euclid step removing q squares of side y
  • indigo rectangle → (x, y) unknown at compile time

What it hides

Only small inputs fit to scale, a zero side has no area so Div(0) = ℕ is a convention, and “largest tile” can hide the clause that every common tile nests inside g.

Audit

Fixed two wrong statements about 0: “Div(0) = ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}” and “all d ≥ 1” both left out 0, which divides 0. Also fixed: Euclid’s cut lines were dark red, the colour reserved for violations, and the halting state 4×0 was captioned as if it were a 4×4 square.

The same lemma with a d-grid you can drag is §2 of gcd-as-a-type.

05

The loop’s state has a type

angle 05 · state-space invariant · Gemini 3.1 Pro, redrawn for this page · 4 figures

The invariant is the set of states (x, y) with gcd(x, y) = gcd(a, b); every Euclid step stays inside it and moves down, and the exit row meets it in the single cell (g, 0).

Encoding

  • shaded cell → a state (x, y) in the invariant set
  • light arrow → one loop step (x, y) → (y, x mod y)
  • navy rings and arrows → the actual run
  • exit row y = 0 → loop exit; its one shaded cell projects to Gcd(a, b)
  • dark-red exit cells → results a too-weak invariant would allow

What it hides

It shows that the step preserves the set but not why x mod y keeps the common divisors (that is angle 04), and a grid reaches only small numbers.

Audit

The original four figures had correct sets, arrows and runs, but no background, dense arrow fields that hid the set, a clipped label, a near-empty (0, 0) grid, and the whole too-weak invariant painted dark red. They were redrawn from the same design and the same computed sets: lighter arrows from shaded cells only, a separate rays figure, three small multiples, and dark red only on the wrong exit cells.

The interactive state space, with every successor arrow on a toggle, is §4 of gcd-as-a-type.

09

The proof as docked tiles

angle 09 · typing derivation as composed pictures · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Typing Euclid as Gcd(a, b) is a chain of set-to-set judgments joined by containments; the invariant makes every joint fit, and the last one lands in the singleton {gcd}.

Encoding

  • tile → one typing judgment: pre-state set in, post-state set out
  • purple dots on the (x, y) grid → states satisfying the invariant
  • purple ⊆ pill between tiles → output set fits the next input set
  • navy arrows → one concrete run
  • dark-red ⊈ joint with ringed state → the failing joint and its counterexample

What it hides

Each picture checks one input pair on a finite window, so “for every state in the invariant” looks like inspecting a few dots, and the decreasing measure is shown, not proved.

Audit

Three wrong statements fixed, all in fig. 5: an infinite leak set {0, 4, 8, 12, …} was written as four values; the buggy-body witness was drawn on the correct run, not the buggy one, which goes (12, 8) → (4, 4) → (2, 0); and Div(0) was written without 0. Also fixed: a false general claim and a window that made Inv(21, 0) look like one point.

A five-rule version of this derivation with an in-page checker is gcd-foundations.

Part IV · one angle

How it would look in the editor

Codillon draws every instruction’s stack effect as a fraction of small shapes. This angle widens those shapes into number lines so that a refined i32 shows its admitted set, and the result of $gcd becomes a one-slot socket tied to the parameters.

10

The type as a socket

angle 10 · Codillon’s editor idiom · Gemini 4 Argon · 5 figures

Inside Codillon’s stack fractions, Gcd(a, b) is a one-slot socket on the result’s i32 number line, tied to a and b; the right return value seats, anything else spills over the rim.

Encoding

  • cup above the rule / shape below → value consumed / value produced
  • wide number line → a refined i32 (linear near 0, log toward the ends)
  • shaded band or notch → values the refinement admits
  • bold socket tied to a and b → Gcd(a, b), its single value
  • dark-red hatch over the rim → a value outside its type

What it hides

The log wings crush 8, 12, 21, 462 and 1071 into a few pixels; the thin notches beside the socket look admitted but are not; and the fig. 2 listing is abridged, not a runnable program.

Audit

Wrong numbers fixed in fig. 3: Div(462) skipped 6; panel C was titled “zero absorber” (0 is the identity for gcd); Gcd(0, 0) and Div(0) were shaded over all of i32, negatives included. Also fixed: “;;” starts a WAT comment, so “i32.const 2 ;; return” hid the return; ties were indigo (the colour for unknown). Not fixable in place: fig. 2’s listing lacks initialization and block/br/end, so it is labelled abridged.

The real editor idiom these shapes extend is the Refined Codillon walkthrough.

Recommendation

No single picture does everything. The table splits the angles into three jobs. Two or three angles cover each job well:

Teaching the definition

02 strips, then 08 family

The divisor strip is the definition read literally. Div(g) and Div(a) ∩ Div(b) sit as two rows, and both ways to fail are visible: an empty socket (too small) and a spilled pin (not common). It needs no factoring and no ℤ. Follow it with 08 fig. 2 to show that “dependent” means a different singleton for every input. Use 01 or 03 for students who already think in prime factors.

Explaining why Euclid is correct

04 tiling + 05 state space

The tiling is the only picture that shows why a step keeps the common divisors, and it does so without algebra. The state space is the only one that shows the whole loop obligation at once: every arrow stays shaded, every arrow goes down, one exit cell. Together they are the proof. 09’s docked tiles are the better choice once students must find which obligation a bug broke.

Inside the editor

10 socket, opening to 02 and 09

Only 10 fits Codillon’s per-instruction fractions as they are. The result is a socket tied to its parameters, and a wrong return spills. Hovering the socket can open the 02 strip as evidence, and a failing obligation between instructions is 09’s broken ⊈ joint with its witness state.

The others are worth keeping as alternates. 06 is the clearest picture of “refinement = conjunction = intersection”. 07 suits readers who know Bézout. 01 and 03 make “greatest” mean “top”, not “largest”, at the price of factoring.

Appendix

Audit log

Before anything went on this page, every figure was audited. Every number and claim in each SVG was recomputed in Python: divisor sets, gcds, the lattice, Bézout coefficients, tilings, fibers, and invariant sets checked cell by cell. Each figure was also rendered and checked by eye for overlaps and clipping. As a final pass, 202 divisor-set, gcd, remainder and Bézout equalities were extracted from all 49 figures and recomputed; all hold. None of the 49 figures had to be left out. Ten statements were wrong (in angles 02, 04, 09 and 10), and all ten are fixed. About 35 more misled or broke the colour rules; nearly all are fixed, and the rest are noted in captions. Angle 05 was redrawn. The source files are untouched; fixes are applied to copies by scripts.

  • MISLEADING, fixed: three “↑” pointers in fig. 2 sat under the wrong columns; “0 spills” and “0 empty” read as “divisor 0”; one set had two names.
